before.stem: Regarding the trochlear nerve, which of the following statements is CORRECT:
options: The trochlear nerve has both sensory and motor function. 2%
The trochlear nerve innervates the superior rectus muscle. 4%
The trochlear nerve enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
Trochlear nerve palsy results in loss of eyeball adduction. 4%
before.explanation: The trochlear nerve enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure. It has the longest intracranial course. It is a purely motor nerve, which innervates the superior oblique muscle responsible for intorsion, depression and abduction of the eye. Vv

after.stem: Regarding the trochlear nerve, which of the following statements is CORRECT:
options: The trochlear nerve has both sensory and motor function.
The trochlear nerve innervates the superior rectus muscle.
The trochlear nerve has the shortest intracranial course.
The trochlear nerve enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
Trochlear nerve palsy results in loss of eyeball adduction.
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.
after.explanation: CN IV is purely motor, supplies superior oblique, has the longest intracranial course, and enters via the superior orbital fissure.
after.learningNote: CN IV is purely motor, supplies superior oblique, has the longest intracranial course, and enters via the superior orbital fissure.
after.highYieldNote: CN IV is purely motor, supplies superior oblique, has the longest intracranial course, and enters via the superior orbital fissure.

memoryAid.coreFact: CN IV is purely motor, supplies superior oblique, has the longest intracranial course, and enters via the superior orbital fissure.

evidence.externalFinding: NCBI supports the trochlear course and orbital entry.

before.stem: A 55 year old woman presents to ED complaining of vertical diplopia with difficulty walking downstairs. She is tilting her head to one side as she says this helps ease the diplopia. Which of the following extraocular muscles is responsible for this picture:
warnings: No marked correct option was detected.
before.explanation: The superior oblique, innervated by the trochlear nerve, acts to cause intorsion, depression and abduction of the eyeball. In trochlear nerve palsy the patient complains of difficulty reading or walking downstairs and of vertical diplopia. The eye is extorted and may be elevated and the patient may head tilt to the opposite side of the palsy to compensate. Cc | Se Teer Vv

before.stem: Ww A patient presents with spontaneous onset of left sided facial weakness but is otherwise well. He is unable to purse his lips, close his eye fully or raise his eyebrow on the left side, which of the following is the most likely cause:
before.explanation: The most common cause of isolated lower motor neuron (LMN) facial nerve palsy is Bell's palsy. If the damage is peripheral (LMN), the forehead will be involved and there will be an inability to close the eyes or raise the eyebrows. If the damage is central (UMN) there is forehead sparing as the frontalis and orbicularis oculi muscles are innervated bilaterally. Vv

after.stem: A patient presents with spontaneous onset of left sided facial weakness but is otherwise well. He is unable to purse his lips, close his eye fully or raise his eyebrow on the left side, which of the following is the most likely cause:
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.
after.explanation: Bell palsy is the common isolated lower-motor-neuron facial palsy and involves the forehead and eye closure.
after.learningNote: Bell palsy is the common isolated lower-motor-neuron facial palsy and involves the forehead and eye closure.
after.highYieldNote: Bell palsy is the common isolated lower-motor-neuron facial palsy and involves the forehead and eye closure.
after.mnemonic: LMN VII affects the whole side.

memoryAid.coreFact: Bell palsy is the common isolated lower-motor-neuron facial palsy and involves the forehead and eye closure.
memoryAid.mnemonic: LMN VII affects the whole side.

before.stem: A 21 year old female presents to ED with isolated facial nerve palsy. You diagnose Bell's palsy. Which of the following clinical features might you expect on examination:
options: Sensory loss over the cornea and conjunctiva (x) Fixed and dilated pupil 1%
Loss of sensation over the ipsilateral face
warnings: No marked correct option was detected.
before.explanation: The facial nerve innervates the orbicularis oculi, the muscle responsible for closing the eye. The facial nerve is therefore the efferent pathway of the corneal blink reflex. Sensation to the face, and the cornea and conjunctiva is supplied by the trigeminal nerve, which is therefore the afferent pathway of the corneal blink reflex. A fixed dilated pupil, and loss of the accommodation reflex may be seen in palsy of the oculomotor nerve due to loss of innervation of the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle respectively. Cc | Se [seer Vv

after.stem: A 21 year old female presents to ED with isolated facial nerve palsy. You diagnose Bell's palsy. Which of the following clinical features might you expect on examination:
options: Sensory loss over the cornea and conjunctiva
Loss of the corneal blink reflex
Loss of sensation over the ipsilateral face
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.

after.learningNote: CN VII is the efferent corneal-blink limb through orbicularis oculi.

before.stem: The oculomotor nerve supplies all of the following structures EXCEPT for the:
before.explanation: The oculomotor nerve supplies four extraocular muscles - the inferior oblique, superior rectus, inferior rectus and medial rectus muscles, the levator palpebrae superioris muscle, the sphincter pupillae muscle and the ciliary muscle. The superior oblique muscle is innervated by the trochlear nerve, and the lateral rectus muscle by the abducens nerve. Vv

before.stem: w A 28 year old man presents to ED complaining of severe headaches and dizziness. Imaging shows a tumour compressing the hypoglossal canal. Which of the following clinical features would you most expect to see:
options: Uvula deviation away from affected side
Tongue deviation on protrusion towards affected side
before.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve exits the cranial cavity through the hypoglossal canal. Injury to the hypoglossal nerve will result in ipsilateral tongue weakness, atrophy and fasciculations, with tongue deviation on protrusion towards the affected side due to the unopposed action of the opposite genioglossus muscle. Vv
